headings.title: Introduction to Care Homes and Residential Care
headings.content: A **care home** is a residential facility that provides accommodation alongside personal or nursing care for individuals who can no longer live independently, usually older adults or people with chronic disabilities. Unlike independent living communities, care homes offer round-the-clock support with the activities of daily living. Residential care homes focus mainly on personal assistance such as bathing, dressing, and eating. Nursing homes, a specialized type of care home, employ qualified medical personnel to manage complex health needs. These facilities bridge the gap between hospital care and independent home living, offering a stable, structured environment. In Nigeria, the concept of formal residential care is evolving rapidly due to shifting family structures and increased urbanization, moving away from exclusive reliance on informal family caregiving.

headings.title: Types of Care Homes and Levels of Support
headings.content:
Care homes are categorized based on the intensity of medical and social support they provide. Understanding these tiers ensures residents are placed in environments that match their clinical acuity.

- **Residential Care Homes**: Provide meals, housing, and personal care assistance like washing and mobility support.
- **Nursing Homes**: Offer continuous professional nursing oversight alongside personal care for residents with unstable medical conditions.
- **Dementia Specialized Units**: Secured living areas equipped with environmental modifications and specialized staff trained in cognitive impairment behaviors.
- **Respite Care Facilities**: Offer short-term stays to give family caregivers temporary relief from their duties.

headings.title: Regulatory Frameworks and Standards
headings.content: Operating a care home requires strict adherence to regulatory standards to protect vulnerable populations from abuse, neglect, and substandard living conditions. Regulatory bodies inspect facilities regularly to evaluate sanitation, staff-to-resident ratios, fire safety, and nutritional adequacy. In Nigeria, state ministries of health and social welfare, alongside professional boards like the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria, set operational guidelines. Compliance ensures accountability, transparency, and a high quality of life for residents. A common misconception is that private facilities do not require government licensing; however, all residential care establishments must meet baseline statutory health codes before admitting clients.

headings.title: Holistic Assessment of Care Home Residents
headings.content: Admission into a care home triggers a comprehensive, multidisciplinary assessment. Nurses evaluate physical health, cognitive function, psychological well-being, nutritional status, and social history. This baseline evaluation uncovers hidden risks such as potential pressure injuries, malnutrition, or depression. Assessing functional ability helps determine the exact assistance a resident needs with activities of daily living. Nurses utilize validated screening tools, such as the Braden Scale for pressure ulcers and the Mini-Mental State Examination for cognition. Involving the resident and their family during this process builds trust and ensures cultural and personal preferences are respected from day one.

headings.title: Person-Centred Care Planning and Daily Living Activities
headings.content: Person-centred care shifts the focus from institutional routines to the individual's unique preferences, values, and life history. Care plans are living documents co-created with the resident whenever possible. Activities of daily living, encompassing bathing, dressing, toileting, and feeding, are structured to promote maximum autonomy. Instead of doing everything for the resident, nursing staff encourage active participation in tasks they can still perform safely. Respecting personal routines, such as waking times and dietary choices, preserves dignity and reduces behavioral distress in residents with cognitive decline.

headings.title: Medication Management and Safety Protocols
headings.content: Medication administration in care homes carries high risk due to the prevalence of polypharmacy among older adults. Nurses must follow strict safety protocols, including the correct identification of residents before administration and accurate documentation. Routine medication reviews help identify drugs that are no longer necessary or that cause harmful side effects, such as excessive sedation or falls. Storage protocols require all pharmaceuticals to be kept securely, with controlled substances logged under double-lock systems. Nurses must remain vigilant for adverse drug reactions and drug-food interactions, reporting any discrepancies immediately to the attending physician.

headings.title: Interprofessional Collaboration in Residential Settings
headings.content: Providing comprehensive care in a residential home requires seamless teamwork among diverse healthcare professionals. Nurses collaborate daily with physicians, physiotherapists, occupational therapists, dietitians, and social workers. Physiotherapists and occupational therapists help maintain resident mobility and adapt living spaces to prevent falls. Dietitians address nutritional deficiencies and swallowing difficulties. Regular multidisciplinary team meetings allow professionals to review resident progress, adjust care plans, and address emerging health concerns proactively. Effective communication bridges professional gaps and ensures the resident receives coordinated, holistic support.

headings.title: Ethical Legal Issues and End-of-Life Care
headings.content: Care home nurses frequently encounter complex ethical and legal decisions, particularly regarding autonomy, consent, and end-of-life care. Residents have the right to make choices about their treatment, even when those choices conflict with staff recommendations. Advance care directives and living wills guide clinical decisions when a resident loses the capacity to communicate their wishes. Palliative and end-of-life care in residential settings focuses on comfort, pain management, and dignity rather than curative interventions. Nurses support both the resident and their grieving families, ensuring a peaceful and compassionate transition.
